cards.title: 3.1 How Waves are Formed
body: Waves are produced by the friction of the wind passing over the water’s surface.
The wind blowing over a smooth surface of water creates small ripples (small wave or series of tiny waves) that grow into recognizable waves.

cards.title: Waves: fuller notes
body: Waves are formed by **wind** blowing over the sea surface. Their size depends on wind speed, how long it blows and the **fetch** (distance of open water). As a wave reaches shallow
**Constructive waves** are low and gentle with a strong swash: they build beaches. **Destructive waves** are high and steep with a strong backwash: they erode.

cards.title: Coastal waves
body: Waves erode cliffs, transport sediment alongshore (longshore drift), build beaches/spits.
Destructive waves: high energy; constructive: build berms.

cards.title: Coast management intro
body: Hard: seawalls, groynes. Soft: beach nourishment, dunes.
Groynes trap sand moving by longshore drift.

cards.title: Worked example: sequence on a headland
cards.problem: Put these in order of formation and explain: arch, stump, cave, stack.

steps.text: **Cave**: waves erode a weakness in the headland.
**Arch**: the cave is cut right through the headland.

cards.answer: **Stump**: the stack is eroded down to a low rock.

questions.q: All are minor features produced by wave erosion during the process of cliff formation except:
why: The textbook: 'Caves, Blowholes, Arches, and Stacks: These are minor features' formed as waves attack a cliff (cave → blowhole → arch → stack).
Bays (with headlands) are larger features formed where soft rock along a coast is eroded more quickly – not one of the minor cliff features.
